issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette:
Rafiq was 75 when he finally agreed to come in, a married South Asian man who had spent most of his life making pottery with his hands and, until recently, prided himself on still being able to shape clay at his wheel with a steady eye. He had fled as a refugee decades earlier, after a night he still could not lay out in a straight line. When he tried to speak of it, the story broke apart: police in the street, the sound of cars surging and braking, shouting, bodies moving, then a graveyard later, or perhaps a funeral, he was never sure where one piece ended and the next began. He would say only that he could not put the frightening event into words, and that the memory came back more real than ordinary life, not like recalling a past day but like being pulled back into it. Even now, certain moments could bring it roaring close: the sight of a funeral procession, the gate of a cemetery, the solemn drift of grief-related gatherings, the sudden engine of a car passing too near, or a police cruiser idling at the curb. Each of these jolted him into the conviction that he was no longer capable of the life that had once defined him, that he could not deal with even the slightest upset, and that he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next.

Over the years, those appraisals narrowed his world. Rafiq began to judge every unsettling encounter as proof that he was no longer the man who had once worked through hardship without flinching. When a neighbor mentioned a memorial service, he felt a familiar sinking certainty that any brush with mourning or authority might overwhelm him. The same fear rose around the sounds of cars outside his home or shop; a backfiring engine could seem like the start of something dangerous. Because he believed he was too fragile to tolerate even minor conflict, he steered away from disagreement with customers, relatives, and even his wife, swallowing irritation rather than risking an argument. He also avoided positive events that might make him feel happy or hopeful, as if letting himself enjoy anything would make the next blow harder to bear. Those careful efforts to keep life smooth and emotionally contained offered brief relief, but they left him watching every street corner and doorway, constantly scanning for signs of threat, and that constant vigilance fed back into the same belief that he could not cope. The more he organized his days around avoiding upset, the more he came to see himself as diminished, less and less capable of the work and steadiness that had once given him dignity.

The memory itself seemed to live inside those patterns. Because the event remained in disconnected pieces, Rafiq relied on scanning and staying guarded to keep the fragments from taking over; if he noticed police before they noticed him, if he could hear car sounds early, if he could step away from funerals or any public grief, he felt he might stay one step ahead of the terror. But the effort never fully settled him. Instead, each avoided street, each declined invitation, each quiet yielding in the face of possible disagreement reinforced his sense that he was in danger and not up to meeting it. That made the memory return with even greater force, vivid and bodily, and in turn the old scenes became more potent triggers. A funeral passing his route to the pottery district could leave him shaking for hours. A police presence near the shop made him leave the wheel unfinished, palms damp with the sense that something terrible was about to happen. Even a hopeful family celebration could unsettle him, because he had come to believe that feeling glad was itself risky, an opening for loss.

Rafiq’s days had gradually become smaller. He kept working, but only with great effort, and he had started turning down events that might have brought him pleasure or family closeness. He avoided any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even when a customer overstepped or a relative asked a hard question. His wife noticed that he sat near the door, eyes moving from window to window, as if a threat might appear between one breath and the next. He did not describe nightmares or anything dramatic; what stood out in session was how little room he felt he had for ordinary disturbance, and how quickly any sign of danger, loss, or conflict collapsed into the same old certainty that he was finished. By the time he sought help, it was not because the memory had become clearer, but because it had become harder to live around. He feared that if he stayed this guarded much longer, he would lose the last pieces of the life and craft that still mattered to him, yet he was also afraid that letting his guard down would let the past flood back in.
